title: Is Clozapine the Best Medicine for Schizophrenia?
subtitle: "I thought I was going to be a schizophrenia researcher" and other stories.
body_html:
The Frontier Psychiatrists newsletter was created by . It was an adjunct to our hit Clubhouse Creator First show. D-list internet celebrities— that is us. But she came up with the name (The Frontier Psychiatrists) and created the newsletter as a chronicle of the show.

Its current editor-in-chief, , was similarly brought into being—as a professional—thanks to her influence. Carlene—for those just getting started here, she’s my wife—has a great sense of what people are capable of. Carlene imagined me as a public-facing educator, not just a scientist in a “bowels-of-the-hospital” science lab. And here I am, educating my readers about drugs! Every story has a beginning, and mine starts with antipsychotic medicines…I met Carlene when I was presenting a poster about these medicines at the AACAP meeting at Disney World.

At the time Carlene and I met in 2013, I had planned on a career as a schizophrenia researcher. Today, I tell a story of a schizophrenia medicine called clozapine, my first love in science. I wrote a prior article about its history, which is available here.

My area of research interest was schizophrenia1. Many people who “get into” research do so because of the mentors they have. Charismatic individuals with passion are seductive—they want more scholars to dedicate themselves to their passion! I was blessed with an abundance of research mentorship with a high degree of both passion and expertise in schizophrenia—and, particularly, its then-definitive treatments, such as clozapine and long-acting injectable medicines. There was also a focus on mitigating the adverse effects of such therapies. John Kane, M.D., the scientist who brought Clozapine back to life. It had been taken off the market after its introduction for life-threatening side effects, but Dr. Kane got it through the FDA because it worked better than existing treatments.2. He was my department chair. Christoph Correll, M.D., was my mentor in the research track and made his bones by studying antipsychotic-induced weight gain.3

Perhaps most formative was my relationship with Peter Manu, M.D. He is a deeply gracious internal medicine physician who—on my very first rotation in residency—encouraged Deepak Sarpal, M.D., and myself to complete a review on the effects of Clozapine rechallenge—getting the med again if one had a problem the first time—after life-threatening adverse events.4

We were on morning rounds on a bright, warm morning in July, 2011. In the course of our ordinary work, we were evaluating a patient who was suffering from symptoms of schizophrenia. He had done well on clozapine—a medicine approved for the treatment of schizophrenia when nothing else had helped. He had a drop in white blood cells, and the drug was stopped in keeping with the monitoring guidelines. Now, this person was in the hospital again. Could he be given the medicine that had helped him again safely? We knew the standard answer was “no.” Dr. Manu encouraged us to look into the data and find the answer ourselves. Deepak and I spent a few weeks digging.

Clozapine comes with a rare adverse effect—in a tiny fraction of patients, the medicine can cause a potentially fatal drop in a specific kind of vital white blood cells called granulocytes. This effect, agranulocytosis, is feared among psychiatrists, and we had a whole Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) to address it, with required monitoring. This drug, clozapine, set the standard for such REMS programs, which are now much more common for other medicines like accutane and esketamine. This risk of immunodeficiency can be monitored, and that monitoring is baked into our standards of care. Virtually no one dies from this adverse event today. And many, many people live long, healthy, and productive lives because of clozapine. It’s that good. But after someone has already had a life-threatening adverse event—could we imagine giving the drug again?

After a few weeks of scouring the literature, Deepak and I could find no evidence that anyone had ever died—the feared outcome—after being given clozapine again. Most people could tolerate the medicine again if the initial drop in white cells were mild, and even some had success even if it was severe. It was possible that our patient could get his life back, and it was safe (enough) to consider rechallenge with clozapine.

The data supported another trial of clozapine with appropriate monitoring. Dr. Manu noted this was important. It was a contribution to science. We should write it up—and gave us almost a week off of our routine duties to get it done. To this day, this paper is my most impactful, with hundreds of citations.

As my colleague Chris Aiken, M.D., pointed out to me the other night at our Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment event, in schizophrenia, rapid means getting a patient on clozapine in the first 3 years of the illness if they fail first-line treatment.5

This isn’t done regularly. Only a fraction of patients who should be prescribed clozapine have that occur, even in specialized settings working with First Episode Psychosis patients:

A significant proportion (30.2%) of patients in this cohort were treatment-resistant and eligible for clozapine. However, only 7.8% of the sample received clozapine, indicating that this medication was underprescribed.6

The benefits of clozapine, for those who experience it, don’t “poop-out”—they persist, and many individuals who might otherwise have been crippled go on to live full, rich lives:

A significant improvement was observed between the pre-clozapine and the first "on-clozapine" evaluation. This improvement was paralleled by a remarkable conversion of schizophrenia from "active" (mostly paranoid) into "residual" in 70% of all patients. Eight patients became functionally productive to the point of being capable of living an independent life…

The authors of this paper (from Brazil) conclude:

Clozapine is a safe and effective drug for patients with severe schizophrenia who have failed to improve on other antipsychotic drugs. Clozapine's maximal benefit is established by the end of the first year of treatment and continues unabated for many years thereafter.7

Other authors have found that in long-term use, Clozapine leads to not only a better quality of life but also a heck of a lot less “wanting to die”:

Quality of Life Scale (QLS) total improved by 72% at the last follow-up, with 24% of patients rated as having "good" functioning compared with 0% at baseline. Suicidal thoughts/behavior was significantly reduced at the last follow-up from the baseline.8

Clozapine is the only medicine with FDA approval for reducing the risk of suicidal behavior:

From the FDA:

Clozaril is indicated for reducing the risk of recurrent suicidal behavior in patients with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who are judged to be at chronic risk for reexperiencing suicidal behavior, based on history and recent clinical state. Suicidal behavior refers to actions by a patient that put him/herself at risk for death. The effectiveness of Clozaril in reducing the risk of recurrent suicidal behavior was demonstrated over a 2 year treatment period in the InterSePT Trial (see Clinical Trials Data under Clinical Pharmacology). Therefore, Clozaril treatment to reduce the risk of suicidal behavior should be continued for at least 2 years.

On a personal note, suicidal ideation and behavior is a miserable and often terrifying experience. Reducing these behaviors also reduces suffering in a way that matters for patients, families, and doctors. As my friend Chris Aiken, M.D. underscored, it’s better not to wait—starting clozapine sooner in the course of schizophrenia improves the chances of getting its benefits:

In patients with a delay in initiating clozapine of ≤2.8 years and a delay in initiating clozapine of > 2.8 years, the response rates were 81.6% and 30.8% (risk ratio=2.65; 95% confidence interval, 1.80, 3.63), respectively. Clinicians should reduce the delay in initiating clozapine to less than 3 years to improve symptomatic outcomes.

It’s over 2.5x better to start the medicine sooner—which is only initiated after one or more failed trials of less risky antipsychotics or, perhaps, Cobenfy these days.

This was—and is—a remarkable treatment for people who need their lives to be better, less full of horror, and healthier over the long term. Although it should go without saying, schizophrenia impacts 1% of the population, and these individuals deserve dignity and the best treatment available. After the first drug we try, if they aren’t well, we should move to clozapine next.

This is as opposed to endlessly futzing around with drugs that are unlikely to work9—and this is the majority of patients. Let me propose a slogan:

“Clozapine: Get On With It, Already.”

Share

1

I had signed up for a completely “unnecessary” 4th year of general psychiatry residency—most child psychiatrists do three years of psychiatry training and two more years of child psychiatry fellowship. This is opposed to four total years of general psychiatry residency. I used that extra year, which isn’t needed for board certification, for a “research track” experience. I honestly wouldn’t recommend this approach to anyone today. It’s more research experience to do the whole shebang in 5 years and add another T32 research fellowship at the end, but at least you can work as an attending psychiatrist nights and weekends, which helps pay down our ample debt faster.

2

3

4

5

6

7

de Oliveira-Souza, R., Marrocos, R. P., & Moll, J. (2008). Clozapine for severe (“kraepelinian”) schizophrenia: Sustained improvement over 5 years. Dementia & Neuropsychologia, 2(1), 71.

8
